lines.text: Lesson twenty-six: understanding AI decisions. Phase 6, XORA Intelligence.
In T25 you saw how XORA analyses a coin. Now: what does it decide, and why?
For each coin, XORA's engine gives one of three answers. It's not a prediction.
It is the result of rule-based checks.
Answer one: BUY, also called long. You gain if the price rises after you enter.
Answer two: SELL, also called SHORT. You gain if the price falls after you enter.
Answer three: NO TRADE. You stand aside and wait. No setup right now.
A plan is for one candle only: BUY if price trades above 60,120, for example.
How does XORA choose? With checks: yes-or-no tests written as rules in code.
Like a pilot's checklist before take-off. Each item is ticked, or it isn't.
The filters use common techniques: trend, support and resistance, volume, momentum and more.
Confidence is a score for how much evidence agrees with a setup.
Think of witnesses. One witness is weak. Several who agree, independently, are stronger.
Each confirmation that agrees raises the score. A check that disagrees, or has no data, adds nothing.
In the app, this is the ENTRY CHECKLIST. Each check shows a tick or a cross.
BUY shows 72% / 60%: a score of 72, against your minimum of 60. It meets it, so it's READY.
SELL shows 55% / 60%. Below your minimum, so no READY badge, and no sell.
Fictional numbers, of course.
A common mistake: reading 72% as a 72% chance of winning.
That's wrong. The app itself says: confidence is evidence strength, not a chance of winning.
A READY trade can still lose. Every trade needs a stop and a size you can afford.
Even a READY setup must pass safety checks. Any one of them can block the trade.
Is the spread too wide? Is the market too thin? Is the data stale, or the plan expired?
Is the stop too tight or too wide? Is there too little room to the next level?
If any check fails: no trade.
Markets are often unclear. Price chops sideways, and the checks disagree.
Then XORA shows No trade, with its reasons, and keeps watching. That's a good outcome.
No trade means no loss. Waiting is a decision, and often the wise one.
In Trade Settings you choose a confidence threshold: Enter only at or above. Default: 50%.
From 50% up, XORA uses several indicators for confirmation. Higher means more must agree.
45% is special. It's not 45% confidence: XORA then looks for chart-pattern setups instead.
Entry modes change the filters: Basic looks for chances, Secure wants more confirmation, Advanced adds more.
Auto trade approval is off by default. A triggered setup waits for you to tap Approve.
Approve before its one-minute candle ends, or it expires.
With auto approval on, the engine enters by itself, within your settings.
Your own BUY or SHORT tap is always your call. The sheet says if the engine agrees.
Your turn. Read the checklist and choose an answer. Pause if you need more time.
Answer B. 68 is below your minimum of 70, so no READY, and no trade.
And C is wrong: confidence is not a chance of winning.
Before you trust any decision, know its limits.
XORA does not guarantee profits. Rules can be wrong, and losing trades happen.
Prices can jump past a stop, fees add up, and leverage makes losses bigger.
So practise in DEMO first. This is education, not financial advice.
Recap. XORA gives three answers: BUY, SELL or SHORT, or NO TRADE, from rule-based checks.
Confidence is evidence strength, checked against your minimum. Safety checks can still say no.
Check yourself: 80% / 60%, but the spread is too wide. Trade? No, the safety check blocks it.
